migrationNotes: Spine: a teacher cannot hand out stickers until she has worked out the class average, and the same two passes are followed in SQL as the inside query grows from one number to a list, a yes-or-no test and an answer that changes with each row.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-ask-a-query-inside-a-query-8 (what the subquery in the average comparison supplies). The first screen teaches it and -1 tests it.

lesson.title: Use one query to define another

lead.text: The teacher's two passes carry straight over into SQL. We'll use the shop's orders again: six orders, five with a known amount (80, 20, 80, 40 and 20) and one, order 106, whose amount isn't known yet. The question is which orders are worth more than the average order.

The first pass is a query of its own: SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders. It adds up the known amounts, 240 altogether, and divides by the five orders that have one, which gives 48. An order with an unknown amount is left out of both the sum and the count.

afterFigure.text: Now for the second pass. Write the first query in brackets and put it where the number would go: WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders). A query written inside another one like this is called a subquery. SQL runs the subquery first and gets one number back. The outer query then compares every order with that number, just as the teacher compared each score with the figure in her margin.
A subquery that returns one number is the simplest case. Sometimes the first pass has to produce a whole list instead, and after two questions on the average the lesson turns to that.

queries.label: The average on its own
queries.sql: SELECT AVG(amount) AS average FROM orders;

queries.label: What the average is built from
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

lead.text: Do it the teacher's way. Find the average first, then compare each score with it.
The shop's orders get the same treatment. The subquery works out the average amount first, and the outer query keeps the orders above it. Think about which of the five known amounts pass.

reveal.text: You compared each amount with the average the subquery found. An amount equal to it would not pass a strict comparison.

queries.label: Above the average
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Strictly above 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 80 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: So far the inside query has handed back one number. It can just as well hand back a column of values, and the outer query can then check whether a row's value is on that list. The test is written IN: a row passes when its value is among the values the subquery returns.

Suppose the shop wants every order placed by a customer in the North region. The orders table doesn't know where anyone lives. It stores only a customer_id, and the region sits in the customers table. So the first pass looks up the North customers with SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'North' and gets a short list of ids. The second pass keeps any order whose customer_id is on that list.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the first pass alone, for two regions. IN asks only whether a value is on the list. A long list never repeats an order, and the outer result still has one row per order. The amount plays no part in the test. Whenever a customer is on the list, all of that customer's orders are kept, including any whose amount is unknown.

queries.label: The North list
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE region = 'North' ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The South list
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE region = 'South' ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Find the North customers first, then count the orders that point at them.

reveal.text: You found the customers first and then their orders. An order with an unknown amount still counts: IN looks at the customer.

queries.label: North customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'North') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: South customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'South') ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Sometimes the outer query doesn't need the matching values at all. It only needs to know whether there are any. Take the shop's customers and ask which of them have placed at least one order. The question is put to one customer at a time.

EXISTS puts that question in brackets. For each customer, the subquery looks through the orders for one whose customer_id is that customer's id, and EXISTS says yes as soon as it finds a single row. Ada has two orders, and she is still listed once, because the question is only whether a match is there. The number of matches never changes the answer. Put NOT in front and the test flips, keeping the customers for whom the search comes back empty.

afterFigure.text: The first query in the figure keeps Ada, Ben and Cy. The second keeps Dee, who has placed nothing. Look at the inside query: it mentions c.id, the id of the customer being asked about at that moment. That means it can't be run once and then forgotten. It has to be run again for each customer, and a later screen comes back to why that matters.

queries.label: At least one order
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: No orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: Ada has two orders in the table, yet the EXISTS query lists her on a single line.

steps.headline: An inside query that changes with the row

lead.text: The inside query for EXISTS used the customer being asked about, so its answer depended on which customer that was. A subquery that refers to a value from the current row of the outer query is called correlated. It can't be worked out once in advance, as the average could, so SQL works it out again for every outer row.

Some comparisons need exactly that. Instead of comparing each order with the average for everyone, compare it with the average for its own customer. Ada's orders are 80 and 20, an average of 50, so her 80 is above her own average and her 20 is below it. Ben's are 80 and 40, an average of 60. Cy has a single known amount, 20, which is its own average.

afterFigure.text: Only orders 101 and 103 pass, Ada's 80 and Ben's 80. Cy's order fails because an amount equal to the average is not above it. A strict greater-than never lets equal values through, which is worth remembering for the next question.

queries.label: Each customer's average
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS average FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Above their own customer's average
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.amount FROM orders AS o WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount) FROM orders AS i WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id) ORDER BY o.id;

lead.text: Now compare each order with the average for its own item, not its own customer. Desk, Book and Lamp each have an average of their known amounts.

reveal.text: You compared each amount with its own item's average. Every known amount equals that average, and equal is not above.

queries.label: Above overall average
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Above its item average
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, o.item, o.amount FROM orders AS o WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount) FROM orders AS i WHERE i.item = o.item) ORDER BY o.id;

lesson.orientation: Use scalar subqueries, IN and EXISTS without multiplying the outer result.
lesson.reviewLabel: Use one query to define another
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A teacher has marked six tests. The scores are 10, 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90, and she has promised a sticker to everyone who scored above the class average. She can't tell who has earned one by reading down the list, because she doesn't yet know what the average is.

So she works in two passes. First she adds the scores up, divides by six and jots the answer in the margin. Only then does she go back to the top and compare each pupil's score with the number in the margin. The first pass is there to feed the second.

A database has the same difficulty. Asking for the orders above the average order needs the average before a single order can be judged. SQL lets you write the first pass inside the second. This lesson starts with the simplest case. The inside query hands back one number, and the lesson builds up from there.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write queries that take their comparison from another query placed inside them.

recap.keyIdea: A subquery supplies a value, a list or a yes-or-no test to an outer query. A correlated one is worked out again for each outer row.

blocks.text: You found 3 pupils above a class average of 60 and 2 orders above the shop's average of 48. North customers had 4 orders, and no order sat strictly above the average for its own item.

recap.nextHook: A subquery lets one question borrow the answer to another. Two questions can also share a page, as when a head teacher wants the chess club's pupils and the drama club's pupils on a single list. The next lesson stacks two results into one.

questions.prompt: How many orders have an amount greater than AVG(amount) over all orders?
hints: Calculate the average of known amounts.
Use a strict greater-than comparison.
The threshold is 240 ÷ 5; test each known amount against it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known average is 48; orders 101 and 103 each have amount 80.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The subquery gives the average, and only the amounts above it pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every known amount. Only those above the average pass.
Check each known amount against the average. More than one is above it.

questions.prompt: How many orders belong to customers in the North region?
hints: Find customer ids in North first.
Count their orders even when an amount is missing.
North's customer ids are 1 and 3; each contributes two orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Customers 1 and 3 are North; each has two orders.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The subquery lists the North ids, and IN keeps every order that points at one of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customers. Count the orders they placed.
That is every order. Only North customers count.
That drops an order because its amount is unknown. IN looks at the customer, not the amount.

questions.prompt: Why does EXISTS return Ada once even though she has two orders?
hints: It tests existence without adding each matching subquery row to the outer result.

acceptedIdeas: The outer query has one row per customer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: EXISTS asks whether any matching order exists for each outer customer row. It does not create one outer row per match, so Ada appears once.

choices.label: The outer query has one row per customer

questions.onCorrect: The outer query has one row per customer. EXISTS only tests whether a match is there.

misconceptions.feedback: EXISTS never deletes anything. It only tests.
It does not skip rows. It only asks whether any row exists.

questions.prompt: How many orders are strictly above the average for their own item?
hints: Compare within each item group.
Equality does not pass a strict greater-than condition.
Each known amount equals its item's mean. Test whether equality satisfies a strict > comparison.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Desk amounts equal 80, Book amounts equal 20 and Lamp's known amount equals 40; each equals its item average.

questions.onCorrect: 0. Each known amount equals its item's average, and equal is not above.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are above the overall average. Each is only equal to its own item's average.

questions.prompt: Three customers have zero, one and four orders. How many customers pass EXISTS for an order?
hints: EXISTS asks whether there is at least one match.
Count customers with a nonzero number of orders.
Mark each customer whose order count is positive, then count marked customers once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two customers have at least one order; the number of matches does not duplicate them.

questions.onCorrect: 2. EXISTS needs at least one order, and it counts each customer once.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customer with no orders. EXISTS needs at least one match.
That adds up the orders. EXISTS counts customers, once each.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a subquery that refers to a value from the current outer row?
hints: Its condition depends on which row the outer query is considering.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A correlated subquery uses a value from the current outer row. Its meaning depends on which outer row is being considered.

questions.onCorrect: correlated. Its condition depends on the outer row, so it is run for each of them.

misconceptions.feedback: Nested only says where it sits. The word wanted describes how it uses the outer row.
Scalar describes a single value coming back. The word wanted is about depending on the outer row.

questions.prompt: Six pupils score 10, 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90, and everyone above the class average gets a sticker. How many pupils get a sticker?
hints: Find the class average first.
Add the scores and divide by how many there are.
Count the scores above that average, not equal to it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The scores add up to 360, so the average is 60. The scores above it are 70, 80 and 90.

questions.onCorrect: 3. You worked out one value first and then compared every score with it. A subquery does the same inside a query.

misconceptions.feedback: A score equal to the average is not above it.

questions.prompt: What does the subquery in WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) supply?
hints: How many numbers does AVG return?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AVG returns a single number, and the outer condition compares each amount with it.

questions.onCorrect: A subquery in parentheses can supply a value or a set to the outer query. Here it supplies one number.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the subquery returns a single number, not rows to join.
A subquery supplies values, not column names.

questions.prompt: Five customers have 0, 2, 0, 0 and 5 orders. How many customers pass NOT EXISTS for an order?
hints: NOT EXISTS keeps a customer when the inner query finds no order.
Which customers have no order at all?
Count the customers with zero orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three customers have no order, so NOT EXISTS keeps three.

questions.onCorrect: 3. NOT EXISTS keeps a customer exactly when the inner query finds nothing for them.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customers who have orders. NOT EXISTS keeps those with none.
